Output chatter in learned proposals is a related failure. Stochastic sampling can produce successive chunks whose every sample satisfies position and velocity limits while the commanded acceleration reverses sign rapidly, and each reversal asks the drive for a torque reversal, with the current transitions and $I^2R$ heating that follow if the drive tracks it (@sec-body-actuator-limits).[^fn-hw-thermal-derating] The systems engineer budgets that variation as actuator thermal rise and transmission fatigue, not as perceptual roughness; a trajectory that excites structural resonances or exceeds the drive's thermal limits is infeasible however closely its waypoints follow the task. Even a candidate that passes every internal and seam check must still provide for a replacement that never arrives.

[^fn-hw-thermal-derating]: **Actuator Thermal Derating**\index{Actuator thermal derating!physics}: Joule heating ($I^2R$) in the windings raises stator temperature, and past its limit degrades magnet flux and insulation, so motor controllers enforce derating curves that throttle continuous torque. A velocity profile that ignores this governor meets a mid-trajectory current limit and loses tracking.

## Behavior at the Seam {#sec-planning-behavior-seam}

The transition seam between consecutive action chunks is where physical AI systems face their greatest operational vulnerability. If upstream neural inference encounters scheduling delays, bus stalls, or unhandled exceptions, the execution runtime must manage the seam without violating kinodynamic limits or exhausting mechanical stopping clearance.

### The two-tier deadline hierarchy and commitment cutoffs {#sec-planning-two-tier-deadlines}

Managing motion continuity across chunk transitions requires an explicit, multi-tiered hierarchy of real-time deadlines. In receding-horizon planning, a system cannot simply execute an action chunk until its final setpoint and abruptly decide what to do next; by the time the trajectory runs out of points, physical velocity is nonzero and mechanical inertia makes a collision-free stop impossible. Instead, the runtime establishes a strict two-tier deadline structure governed by monotonic hardware clocks: a soft *blend deadline* ($t_{\mathrm{blend}}$) by which a candidate successor chunk should arrive to enable smooth trajectory blending, and a hard *commitment cutoff* ($t_{\mathrm{commit}}$) at which the controller must unconditionally revoke nominal tracking and activate a verified stopping suffix if no successor has been admitted.

To see how this deadline hierarchy safeguards physical execution during inference hiccups, suppose the chunk policy stalls while the arm is reaching toward the mug. On this machine the shared lease ends the wait `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` after the last admission, and the arm enters its state-matched fallback along the renewal-to-onset path of @sec-planning-handoff. Crucially, all deadline evaluations and timeout checks execute strictly within the **MCU monotonic hardware clock domain**, completely insulated from host operating system freezes, NTP time steps, or Linux scheduler jitter. The record's own deadlines decide how long any lease could be allowed to run, because until the stop begins the arm keeps moving, and every millisecond the MCU waits is travel its stop can no longer use. Let the lease run to its ceiling, then, so that the blend deadline $t_{\mathrm{blend}}$ passes with no replacement admitted. The four deadlines of @sec-planning-handoff, compared in the MCU monotonic clock with $t_{\mathrm{intent\_exp}}$, now decide what happens. A replacement may still be admitted until $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$, the entry of the matched stop suffix, whose duration is $T_{\mathrm{stop}}=t_{\mathrm{stop\_end}}-t_{\mathrm{commit}}$. It must pass the full admission check before that cutoff; a late host progress report has no authority.

### The C$^2$ stopping suffix and effective deceleration penalty {#sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix}

A moving robot carries continuous momentum. If an emergency brake uses an idealized constant-deceleration profile ($a(t) = -a_{\text{brake}}$), the commanded acceleration steps discontinuously from zero to $-a_{\text{brake}}$ at $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$, and steps discontinuously back to zero when velocity reaches zero. This instantaneous switch demands an infinite jerk impulse ($\dddot{q} = \infty$) and an instantaneous step jump in actuator braking torque ($\Delta\tau = J_{\mathrm{eff}} a_{\text{brake}}$). On a mobile base, this torque shock breaks tire traction, skidding the wheels across warehouse epoxy; on an articulated arm, it violently jerks the payload, risking gripper slippage or structural damage.

To brake non-destructively, the deceleration profile must ramp smoothly up and down with unbroken $C^2$ continuity. For a cruise entry with position $q(t_{\mathrm{commit}}) = q_c$, cruise speed $v_c > 0$, and zero entry acceleration, a $C^2$ position-and-velocity-matched stop over duration $T$ parameterizes motion via the normalized time variable $u = (t - t_{\mathrm{commit}}) / T \in [0, 1]$:

$$q(u) = q_c + v_c T \left(u - u^3 + \frac{1}{2} u^4\right), \qquad 0 \le u \le 1$$ {#eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix}

Differentiating @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix with respect to physical time $t$ ($\frac{d}{dt} = \frac{1}{T} \frac{d}{du}$) yields the continuous velocity, acceleration, and jerk profiles:

$$\begin{aligned}
\dot{q}(u) &= v_c \left(1 - 3u^2 + 2u^3\right) \\
\ddot{q}(u) &= -\frac{6 v_c}{T} u(1 - u) \\
\dddot{q}(u) &= -\frac{6 v_c}{T^2} (1 - 2u)
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-plan-c2-derivatives}

Evaluating the profiles of @eq-plan-c2-derivatives at the boundaries confirms their physical properties:

- At entry ($u = 0$, $t = t_{\mathrm{commit}}$): $q(0) = q_c$, $\dot{q}(0) = v_c$, and $\ddot{q}(0) = 0$. The suffix seamlessly matches steady-state cruise with zero acceleration step.
- At rest ($u = 1$, $t = t_{\mathrm{commit}} + T$): $q(1) = q_c + \frac{1}{2} v_c T$, $\dot{q}(1) = 0$, and $\ddot{q}(1) = 0$. The mechanism reaches a complete, stable standstill with zero residual acceleration shock.

The deceleration profile $\ddot{q}(u)$ forms a symmetric inverted parabola over $u \in [0, 1]$. Its maximum deceleration occurs at the maneuver midpoint $u = 0.5$ (where $u(1-u) = 1/4$):

$$a_{\mathrm{peak}} = \max_{u \in [0, 1]} |\ddot{q}(u)| = \frac{6 v_c}{T} \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1.5 v_c}{T}$$

Holding the peak at the robot's physical braking limit $a_{\mathrm{peak}} \le a_{\mathrm{brake}}$ fixes the required stopping duration:

$$T = \frac{1.5 v_c}{a_{\mathrm{brake}}}$$

The total stopping distance traveled during the suffix is the integral of velocity over $[0, T]$:

$$d_{C^2} = q(1) - q(0) = \frac{1}{2} v_c T = \frac{1}{2} v_c \left(\frac{1.5 v_c}{a_{\mathrm{brake}}}\right) = \frac{3}{4} \frac{v_c^2}{a_{\mathrm{brake}}} = 1.5 \left(\frac{v_c^2}{2 a_{\mathrm{brake}}}\right)$$

This 50 percent increase in braking distance is the **Kinematic Deceleration Tax**: smooth, non-destructive braking always costs $1.5\times$ the distance of an idealized constant-deceleration step ($d_{C^2} = 0.75 \frac{v_c^2}{a_{\mathrm{brake}}}$ vs. $0.5 \frac{v_c^2}{a_{\text{brake}}}$). In a stopping budget, the $C^2$ suffix behaves like constant braking at $a_{\text{eff}}=a_{\text{brake}}/1.5$. Any autonomous machine that sizes its sensor horizon or clearance margins using freshman physics ($v^2 / 2a$) will breach its safety envelope during smooth stops. A nonzero measured entry acceleration requires a general quintic matching the actual $(q,\dot q,\ddot q)$ at entry and zero terminal velocity and acceleration; the permission path checks its interior speed, acceleration, jerk, torque, and clearance.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-c2-stop-clearance
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ C2 STOP SUFFIX ON THE WAREHOUSE MOBILE MANIPULATOR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-behavior-seam (arm case, base budget row, commitment
# │          counterfactual, checkpoint), @sec-planning-summary.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the C2 suffix for the arm and the base and add its term to the
# │          base's stopping budget.
# │ Show:    Arm 150 mm suffix and 90 mm margin; a lease run 200 ms past
# │          commitment breaches the 300 mm clearance by 110 mm; base
# │          1125 ms / 843.75 mm at 1.5 m/s, +281.25 mm, running total
# │          1194.15 mm past 1.10 m.
# │ How:     RM/AISLE registry fields; calc_c2_stop_suffix for each suffix;
# │          calc_safe_stopping_distance with a_brake (Ch8 total) and with
# │          a_eff = a_brake/1.5 (Ch11 total).
# │
# │ Note:    No aisle-speed value appears here; @sec-enforcement owns the
# │          finished budget (canon round 3, F6).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg, millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PlanningC2Stop:
    """C2 stop suffix for the machine's arm and base, and the budget row it adds."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    # Arm: free-space stop from the machine's TCP speed limit.
    v_arm = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen; registry
    t_blend = PlanningArmTimeline.t_blend  # category: chosen; calc-planning-arm-timeline
    t_commit = PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit  # category: chosen
    t_plan_exp = PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp  # category: derived
    t_arm_stop = PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop  # category: illustrative
    d_arm_clear = PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear  # category: illustrative; obstacle clearance, calc-planning-lease-rule
    t_wait = 200 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; tracking authority run past commitment
    # Base: the stop at the rack end.
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative; registry drive limit
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative; credible deceleration, loaded, dry floor
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived; total pre-brake delay
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative; rack-end clear distance

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    a_arm_peak = (1.5 * v_arm / t_arm_stop).to(ureg.meter / ureg.second**2)
    arm_suffix = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_arm, a_arm_peak)
    arm_cruise = (v_arm * (t_commit - t_blend)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    arm_stop_dist = arm_suffix["distance"].to(ureg.millimeter)
    arm_total = arm_cruise + arm_stop_dist
    arm_margin = d_arm_clear - arm_total
    t_stop_end = (t_commit + arm_suffix["duration"]).to(millisecond)
    late_cruise_arm = (v_arm * t_wait).to(ureg.millimeter)
    late_breach_arm = late_cruise_arm - arm_margin

    c2_drive = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_drive, a_brake)
    brake_const = (v_drive**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(ureg.millimeter)
    c2_increment = c2_drive["distance"].to(ureg.millimeter) - brake_const
    total_prev = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_drive, tau_delay, a_brake, delta_loc, delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)
    total_new = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_drive, tau_delay, a_brake / 1.5, delta_loc, delta_margin).to(ureg.millimeter)
    excess = total_new - d_clear.to(ureg.millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(a_arm_peak.magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, "arm suffix peak changed")
    check(abs(arm_suffix["duration"].to(millisecond).magnitude - 300.0) < 1e-9, "arm suffix duration changed")
    check(abs(arm_stop_dist.magnitude - 150.0) < 1e-9, "arm suffix distance changed")
    check(abs(arm_cruise.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "arm pre-onset cruise changed")
    check(abs(arm_margin.magnitude - 90.0) < 1e-9, "arm clearance margin changed")
    check(abs(t_stop_end.magnitude - 600.0) < 1e-9, "arm stop end changed")
    check(t_stop_end == PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_end, "C2 arm stop end disagrees with the timeline cell")
    check(t_blend < t_commit < t_plan_exp < t_stop_end, "arm deadline order broken")
    check(
        abs(arm_stop_dist.magnitude - PlanningLeaseRule.arm_stop_dist.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "arm stop disagrees with the lease-rule cell",
    )
    check(
        abs(arm_margin.magnitude - PlanningLeaseRule.commit_margin.to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "arm margin disagrees with the lease-rule cell",
    )
    check(abs(late_cruise_arm.magnitude - 200.0) < 1e-9, "late-commitment arm cruise changed")
    check(abs(late_breach_arm.magnitude - 110.0) < 1e-9, "late-commitment arm breach changed")
    check(abs(c2_drive["duration"].to(millisecond).magnitude - 1125.0) < 1e-9, "C2 duration at drive limit changed")
    check(abs(c2_drive["distance"].to(ureg.millimeter).magnitude - 843.75) < 1e-9, "C2 distance at drive limit changed")
    check(abs(brake_const.magnitude - 562.5) < 1e-9, "constant-deceleration braking changed")
    check(abs(c2_increment.magnitude - 281.25) < 1e-9, "C2 budget increment changed")
    check(abs(total_prev.magnitude - 912.9) < 5e-3, "Ch8 running total changed")
    check(abs(total_new.magnitude - 1194.15) < 5e-3, "Ch11 running total changed")
    check(abs(excess.magnitude - 94.15) < 5e-3, "excess over clear distance changed")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    v_arm_str = fmt_velocity(v_arm)
    t_blend_str = fmt_latency(t_blend, unit=millisecond)
    t_commit_str = fmt_latency(t_commit, unit=millisecond)
    t_plan_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_plan_exp, unit=millisecond)
    t_stop_end_str = fmt_latency(t_stop_end, unit=millisecond)
    t_arm_stop_str = fmt_latency(t_arm_stop, unit=millisecond)
    a_arm_peak_str = fmt_acceleration(a_arm_peak)
    arm_stop_dist_str = fmt_length(arm_stop_dist, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    arm_cruise_str = fmt_length(arm_cruise, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    arm_total_str = fmt_length(arm_total, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    arm_margin_str = fmt_length(arm_margin, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    d_arm_clear_str = fmt_length(d_arm_clear, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    v_drive_str = fmt_velocity(v_drive)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake)
    c2_drive_time_str = fmt_latency(c2_drive["duration"], unit=millisecond, commas=True)
    c2_drive_dist_str = fmt_length(c2_drive["distance"], unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    brake_const_str = fmt_length(brake_const, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    c2_increment_str = fmt_length(c2_increment, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    total_prev_str = fmt_length(total_prev, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=1)
    total_new_str = fmt_length(total_new, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=ureg.meter, precision=2)
    excess_str = fmt_length(excess, unit=ureg.millimeter, precision=2)
    t_wait_str = fmt_latency(t_wait, unit=millisecond)
    late_cruise_arm_str = fmt_length(late_cruise_arm, unit=ureg.millimeter)
    late_breach_arm_str = fmt_length(late_breach_arm, unit=ureg.millimeter)
```

In the worked arm case, the blend deadline is `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_blend_str`, matched commitment `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_commit_str`, nominal setpoint end `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_plan_exp_str`, and stop end `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_stop_end_str`, so $T$ is `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_arm_stop_str`. At the arm's `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_arm_str` Tool Center Point (TCP) speed limit, the suffix's peak deceleration is `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_arm_peak_str` and it travels `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_stop_dist_str`. Clearance is last checked at the blend deadline, so the cruise from `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_blend_str` to physical brake onset at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_commit_str` is charged against that clearance and uses `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_cruise_str`; the full `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_total_str` leaves `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` of the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_arm_clear_str` obstacle clearance. Sensing and model error must still come out of that geometric margin. The stated `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_commit_str` is **physical suffix onset**, so the MCU must close replacement admission and pretrigger any communication or actuator delay $\delta$ by that instant minus $\delta$. If it does not, add $v_c\delta$ of travel and shift the stop end; the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` margin is then smaller. Nominal setpoints end at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_plan_exp_str` while MCU STOP continues to `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_stop_end_str`, and the case assumes that fresh target evidence keeps TRACK valid that long (@sec-planning-goal-to-trajectory).

The operational lifecycle of this deadline structure is illustrated in @fig-11-seam-timeline-fallback, which compares nominal continuous execution against the protected stopping transition on a synchronized MCU timeline:

- **Nominal replacement path (top):** Motion commences at $t=0$. Upstream neural planners target the blend deadline at $t_{\mathrm{blend}} = 240\ \text{ms}$. When a replacement chunk arrives and passes full MCU admission checks before $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$, the new chunk smoothly blends into the trajectory at $t_{\mathrm{blend}}$, refreshing the horizon and extending nominal tracking without deceleration.
- **Physical commitment boundary ($t_{\mathrm{commit}} = 300\ \text{ms}$):** If no successor passes admission by 300 ms, nominal tracking permission is revoked. Even though the current chunk holds nominal setpoints extending to $t_{\mathrm{plan\_exp}} = 320\ \text{ms}$, the controller does not continue tracking toward them. Continuing nominal tracking would consume the deceleration clearance.
- **Protected stopping continuation ($t_{\mathrm{stop\_end}} = 600\ \text{ms}$):** At $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$, the MCU activates its pre-latched $C^2$ stopping suffix. As shown in the lower panel of @fig-11-seam-timeline-fallback, the robot transitions from nominal tracking to the protected STOP regime, executing the 300 ms smooth polynomial deceleration until reaching zero velocity at 600 ms. Notice that the stop continuation safely outlasts both the nominal chunk setpoints ($t_{\mathrm{plan\_exp}}$) and any expiring upstream intent leases.

A stall on this machine never reaches commitment. One permission tick, one bus cycle, and brake onset, `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_dispatch_str` together, put the arm's stop onset `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_path_str` after the last admission, or `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_lease_path_str` of travel at the TCP limit. From zero-acceleration cruise the $C^2$ profile matches the arm at whatever instant it starts, so the state-matched fallback travels the same `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.arm_stop_dist_str` as the matched stop suffix. The renewal-to-onset path therefore uses `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_total_str` of the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear_str` clearance and leaves `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_margin_str`, against `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.commit_margin_str` when the stop begins at commitment. Because stop onset must come by the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_commit_str` commitment, the lease may run at most `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_max_str`.

On the arm, commitment decides whether the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` margin survives. A lease `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_wait_str` longer than the arm's `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_max_str` ceiling would let tracking run that far past commitment, and cruise at the TCP limit would add `{python} PlanningC2Stop.late_cruise_arm_str` before the same stop and breach the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_arm_clear_str` clearance by `{python} PlanningC2Stop.late_breach_arm_str`. A later stop must still match its actual entry state; this counterfactual holds cruise speed constant only to show the lost clearance. An arm that waits that long may already occupy a state from which no admissible control avoids the obstacle.

### Inevitable collision states and physical commitment boundaries {#sec-planning-inevitable-collision-states}

In classical robotic path planning, obstacle avoidance is frequently formulated as a static geometric query: does the robot's physical geometry intersect an obstacle in configuration space at the current instant? In physical AI systems operating with continuous momentum, this static spatial check is dangerously inadequate. A mobile manipulator moving with high velocity and finite actuator braking torque cannot reverse its direction or halt instantaneously. Long before the machine physically touches an obstacle, its combined dynamic state—position, velocity, acceleration, and traction limits—can cross an irreversible boundary beyond which every mathematically possible control trajectory leads inevitably to collision. In dynamic systems and control theory, such states are classified as Inevitable Collision States (ICS).

The commitment deadline $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$ is sized precisely so that the machine initiates braking *before* its dynamic state enters an Inevitable Collision State $\text{ICS}(\mathcal{X}_{\text{obs}})$. If the controller delays braking past commitment in the hope that an overdue replanner will deliver an evasive path, physical momentum carries the machine into an ICS from which no admissible control input can prevent impact.

::: {#dfn-planning-inevitable-collision-state .callout-definition title="Inevitable collision state"}

***Inevitable collision state***\index{Inevitable collision state!definition}\index{Collision avoidance!inevitable collision state} (ICS) is any dynamic plant state $\mathbf{x}(t) \in \mathcal{X}$ from which every physically admissible future control trajectory $\mathbf{u}_{[t, \infty)} \in \mathcal{U}$ inevitably produces collision with an obstacle or constraint boundary:
$$\mathbf{x} \in \text{ICS}(\mathcal{X}_{\text{obs}}) \iff \forall \mathbf{u}(\cdot) \in \mathcal{U}, \; \exists \tau \ge t \text{ such that } \mathbf{x}(\tau) \in \mathcal{X}_{\text{obs}}$$
where $\mathcal{U}$ denotes the admissible control input set bounded by actuator torque, traction, and deceleration limits.

1.  **Significance**: Sets the commitment deadline $t_{\text{commit}}$ in receding-horizon planning; continuing nominal motion past it without an admitted successor can carry the plant into an ICS, and no later replanning can bring it back out.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike static geometric collision checks that evaluate only instantaneous spatial overlap ($\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}_{\text{obs}}$), an ICS identifies dynamically trapped states where current momentum and finite braking torque make future boundary breach physically unavoidable.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Delaying emergency braking in the expectation that an overdue neural planner will complete an evasive path, ignoring that moving mass enters an ICS long before geometric contact occurs.

:::

<!-- fig-alt below hand-types values because fig-alt cannot hold inline python. Keep them in sync with these cell outputs:
     "240 milliseconds" = PlanningC2Stop.t_blend_str
     "300"              = PlanningC2Stop.t_commit_str
     "320"              = PlanningC2Stop.t_plan_exp_str
     "600"              = PlanningC2Stop.t_stop_end_str -->

::: {#fig-11-seam-timeline-fallback fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Nominal tracking and the matched stop suffix**: The worked arm permits a checked replacement before the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_commit_str` physical stop onset. Nominal references would end at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_plan_exp_str`, while the separately authorized, $C^2$ stop reaches rest at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_stop_end_str`. The suffix is matched to the commitment state; earlier invalidation needs the state-matched fallback. All deadlines use the MCU monotonic clock, and physical clearance includes the full response and stop." fig-alt="Timeline distinguishes preferred blend at 240 milliseconds, physical stop commitment at 300, nominal setpoint end at 320, and stop end at 600. A second panel shows tracking transferring to a protected stopping state when no replacement is admitted. The stop can continue after nominal or intent tracking permission ends."}
![](images/svg/fig11_seam_timeline_fallback.svg){width="100%"}
:::

These deadlines and the stop they protect are fixed at admission, before motion begins. The candidate declares payload, contact, effort, and obstacle assumptions. The MCU first validates its fixed header and lineage, then checks the complete bounded trajectory and suffix, including the seam $(q,\dot q,\ddot q)$ against its current encoder state, interior extrema, clearance, stopping distance, and a feasible response from every state reachable before commitment. A scan over $N$ setpoints is $O(N)$, even with a fixed maximum $N$ and measured worst-case execution time; after admission, a distinct $O(1)$ per-tick check reads the current state and local reference. A replacement received after the blend deadline passes the same check with a compressed bridge, whose higher acceleration and torque its extrema must still clear, and if the check cannot finish before commitment the MCU keeps the current record. A candidate received after commitment cannot restore the spent runway.

The planner proposes the suffix, but the MCU latches the validated payload and stop coefficients into protected memory **before** enabling TRACK and selects that resident path at commitment without reading host DRAM, so a host crash, bus stall, or corrupted shared packet cannot erase the stop.[^fn-hw-dma-pingpong] If the measured state falls outside the latched suffix's entry region, the MCU uses the state-matched fallback; torque disable or a spring brake is not a universal substitute for a controlled stop, especially with a suspended load (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder).

[^fn-hw-dma-pingpong]: **Inter-core shared-memory contracts**\index{Inter-processor communication!shared memory}\index{Real-time systems!memory barriers}: A shared-memory implementation needs an ownership protocol, cache maintenance where required, and release/acquire ordering. The MCU validates a completed candidate and copies the admitted plan and stop into protected memory before activation.

### Base stopping budget inflation under gentle deceleration {#sec-planning-base-stopping-budget}

The base of the mobile manipulator stops the same way, and for a reason of its own. The loaded tote rack tolerates the machine's credible deceleration only if that deceleration is reached gradually; a stop that begins and ends at zero acceleration costs half again the distance of an abrupt one at the same peak. That cost now enters the stopping budget. At the drive limit of `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_drive_str`, a suffix that peaks at the credible `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_brake_str` lasts `{python} PlanningC2Stop.c2_drive_time_str` and travels `{python} PlanningC2Stop.c2_drive_dist_str`, against the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.brake_const_str` of constant-deceleration braking in @eq-body-stopping-distance. The suffix therefore adds `{python} PlanningC2Stop.c2_increment_str` to the budget that @sec-perception-transduction-calibration left at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.total_prev_str`, for a running total of `{python} PlanningC2Stop.total_new_str`. That total passes the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance by `{python} PlanningC2Stop.excess_str`.

This `{python} PlanningC2Stop.excess_str` deficit proves that the robot cannot safely cruise at its `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_drive_str` drive limit in this aisle once smooth, non-destructive stopping kinetics are respected. The machine must either derate its maximum operating speed or expand its perception horizon. This intentional deficit sets up the runtime enforcement speed governor in @sec-enforcement. This is the stopping condition of Principle \ref{pri-vol4-irreversibility} with one more term, because a stop the load can tolerate is a longer stop and the distance it adds comes out of the same clear distance. With such a stop the machine can no longer run at its drive limit and still stop short of a person who has stepped out at the rack end. Of the budget's terms, only speed is left to give that distance back, and @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes sets it once the last term is in.

For either body, the admission and fallback decisions in @tbl-11-seam-fallback-hierarchy are distinct from an emergency power cut.

| State                      | Trigger                                                                          | MCU action and required evidence                                                                                                                     |
|:---------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| TRACK, ordinary handoff    | Replacement passes the complete admission check before commitment.               | Latch the new nominal path and its own stop, then transfer at a checked $C^2$ seam.                                                                  |
| TRACK, late candidate      | Candidate arrives after the blend deadline but before commitment.                | Admit only if the compressed bridge, full path, stop, and timing still fit; otherwise keep the current record.                                       |
| STOP, matched suffix       | No successor admitted by commitment.                                             | MCU follows its protected suffix from the validated entry state; nominal tracking may end while STOP continues.                                      |
| STOP, earlier invalidation | Lease lapse, intent expiry, contact, state mismatch, or fault before commitment. | MCU selects the state-matched fallback with reserved clearance.                                                                                      |
| Fault response             | Controlled stop cannot be assured from measured state.                           | Use the machine-specific risk response (which may include drive inhibit, brake, or compliance) only under its validated load and timing assumptions. |

: **Tracking and fallback decisions**: A host crash does not remove a latched stop. TRACK is the nominal mode; STOP is the stop rung of the fallback ladder in @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder. {#tbl-11-seam-fallback-hierarchy tbl-colwidths="[18,29,53]"}

::: {#chk-plan-fallback-clearance-stopping-budget .callout-checkpoint title="Commitment and full stopping clearance"}

Before committing an autonomous machine to an action chunk, verify your understanding of commitment deadlines, stopping budgets, and trajectory continuity:

- [ ] **Deadline distinction**: Can you distinguish nominal setpoint end, physical stop completion, and target-evidence expiry?
- [ ] **Continuous entry**: Why would a constant-deceleration switch fail $C^2$ matching at zero-acceleration cruise entry?
- [ ] **Clearance and latency**: The arm's `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` margin already charges cruise from the blend deadline to commitment. Where must an unreserved delay $\delta$ beyond it be charged, and how much of that margin does $v_c\delta$ consume?

:::

Each row of @tbl-11-seam-fallback-hierarchy presumes that its trigger reaches the MCU in time. A failure can first show itself in the candidate, at the seam, or in the world, and each reaches the MCU on a different schedule.

## Trajectory Planning Failure Modes and Infeasible Seams {#sec-planning-failure-modes}

A plan can become infeasible by execution time. Between synthesis in the learned policy and actuation at the causal boundary (@sec-boundary-causal-boundary), the machine's state drifts, the environment shifts, or the seam between consecutive chunks violates dynamic constraints. Where a failure first becomes visible decides which subsystem holds the signal and how much time it has to detect and reject the plan.

### Pre-execution limit and boundary checkers {#sec-planning-pre-execution-checkers}

Before any trajectory setpoint can influence actuator control registers, the safety MCU screens the proposal through two complementary admission gates:

1.  **Pre-execution Bound Checker:** Evaluates the proposed action chunk in isolation against intrinsic kinematic and dynamic limits, computing margin $M(t) = L_{\mathrm{limit}} - |x(t)|$ across all trajectory points for position $q$, velocity $\dot{q}$, and acceleration $\ddot{q}$. Any sample where $M(t) < 0$ triggers immediate rejection with a diagnostic fault record naming the joint channel, timestamp, and negative margin. Rejection at admission causes no dynamic disturbance because the machine continues executing its previously admitted trajectory.
2.  **Boundary Checker:** Evaluates the transition seam between the currently executing trajectory and the candidate replacement at $t_{\mathrm{seam}}$. It compares state vectors $(\Delta q, \Delta\dot{q}, \Delta\ddot{q})$ against measured joint encoder telemetry and bounds the commanded seam torque request via @eq-plan-seam-torque.

For the CSG-25-50 joint of the seam notebook, counting only its `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.j_reflected_str` reflected rotor inertia over one `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.dt_tick_str` tick and allocating the whole `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_rated_str` repeated-peak rating to this acceleration gives an *idealized ceiling* of `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.dq_ceiling_str` on $\Delta\dot q$. Available margin is smaller after link and payload inertia, gravity, friction, other commanded torque, current rise time, and thermal or bus limits are accounted for. The permission path must use that state-dependent margin and the measured drive response when evaluating a finite bridge. It rejects a direct velocity discontinuity even if its one-tick arithmetic falls below that ceiling; a bounded $C^2$ bridge and its interior checks are still required.[^fn-inc-seam-trip]

[^fn-inc-seam-trip]: **Drive and resonance response**\index{Drivetrain!resonant frequency}\index{Inverter!desaturation trip}: A sharp command can excite a joint's *identified* flexible modes, but their frequencies and damping depend on the transmission and load. Current limiting, desaturation detection, DC-bus response, and shutdown depend on the selected driver and its configuration; see the [TI gate-driver protection description](https://www.ti.com/document-viewer/lit/html/SLVAG18/GUID-1263241E-9C90-419F-B3D8-D2F599BCABEA).

### Runtime tracking monitors and unmodeled contact trips {#sec-planning-runtime-monitors}

Even when candidate chunks pass all pre-execution and boundary checks, real-world disturbances during execution can invalidate physical feasibility. Unexpected contact wrenches, grasped payload slip, or structural deflection can cause the physical plant to diverge from its nominal plan.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-monitor-trip
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RUNTIME MONITOR TRIP THRESHOLDS FOR THE ARM
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-failure-modes (runtime monitors paragraph).
# │
# │ Goal:    Derive the tool-position error trip from the budgeted clearance and
# │          the deflection allowance, beside the unmodeled-contact threshold.
# │ Show:    0.020 m - 0.005 m = 0.015 m; 10 N contact threshold.
# │ How:     Illustrative clearance, allowance, and contact threshold.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_length, fmt_force

class PlanningMonitorTrip:
    """Position-error trip threshold and contact threshold for the arm."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    d_clearance = 0.020 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative; budgeted clearance past the conveyor guard
    d_deflect = 0.005 * ureg.meter  # category: illustrative; payload deflection and gearbox compliance
    f_contact = 10 * ureg.newton  # category: illustrative; unmodeled free-space contact threshold

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    eps_pos = (d_clearance - d_deflect).to(ureg.meter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(eps_pos.magnitude - 0.015) < 1e-12, "position error trip changed")
    check(eps_pos.magnitude > 0, "deflection allowance consumes the clearance")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    d_clearance_str = fmt_length(d_clearance, unit=ureg.meter, precision=3)
    d_deflect_str = fmt_length(d_deflect, unit=ureg.meter, precision=3)
    eps_pos_str = fmt_length(eps_pos, unit=ureg.meter, precision=3)
    f_contact_str = fmt_force(f_contact, precision=0)
```

Even with all pre-execution and boundary checks passed, changes in the physical world can render the plan infeasible. A grasped workpiece can slip from its intended $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ pose, an unmodeled obstacle can enter the workspace, or structural tracking error can accumulate beyond allowable tolerances. **Runtime monitors**\index{Runtime monitor} detect changed-world infeasibility by observing four dedicated signals, comprising joint state divergence, tracking error velocity, unexpected contact wrenches, and the invalidation of the geometric assumptions the record declares (@sec-planning-trajectory-contract). This derivation demonstrates **Spatial Margin Budgeting**: geometric obstacle clearance cannot be allocated entirely to tracking error. Physical compliance and mechanical deflection under load consume clearance before any tracking divergence occurs. The tracking error allowance $\epsilon_{\mathrm{pos}}$ is therefore the total swept-volume clearance less the structural deflection and gearbox compliance allowance $\delta_{\mathrm{deflect}}$. For the mobile manipulator's arm reaching past the conveyor guard, a budgeted swept-volume clearance of `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.d_clearance_str` and an unmodeled payload deflection and gearbox compliance allowance $\delta_{\mathrm{deflect}}$ of `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.d_deflect_str` leave an allowance $\epsilon_{\mathrm{pos}}$ of `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.eps_pos_str`. The allowance caps the tracking bound rather than replacing it. The arm tracker's own validated bound, the arm's instance of the $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$ that @sec-enforcement-handoff validates for the base, must sit inside those `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.eps_pos_str`, and the per-tick check trips on $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$. If measured Cartesian tool-position error $\|\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{tool,actual}}(t)-\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{tool,planned}}(t)\|$ exceeds $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$, or a six-axis force-torque sensor reports an unmodeled `{python} PlanningMonitorTrip.f_contact_str` contact in this free-space example, the monitor revokes nominal tracking and requests the validated state-matched fallback. Actual deceleration begins after the measured detection, dispatch, and actuator response delays.

A plan can also exhaust its nominal references before the next candidate passes admission. The MCU must not wait for the execution pointer to run off the array or treat a final-position hold as a stop. On this machine the chunk lease ends the wait first, and a lease run toward its ceiling reaches the commitment rule of @sec-planning-behavior-seam, which the MCU applies in its own monotonic clock. Complete stopping clearance includes detection, dispatch, actuator response, and motion under the selected profile; an assumed constant deceleration is insufficient for the $C^2$ worked suffix.

Every detector in this section relies on an explicit contract between the trajectory generator and the execution runtime. A plan delivered as a raw list of coordinates, without its valid lifespan, clearance bounds, boundary derivatives, and fallback, leaves the permission path unable to tell whether an ongoing motion remains safe or has drifted into infeasibility.

## The Trajectory Contract {#sec-planning-trajectory-contract}

Each time the chunk policy proposes `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.n_horizon_str` new setpoints for the reach toward the mug, the permission path must decide whether to admit them without asking the planner anything. The formal **Trajectory Plan** record (`TrajectoryPlan`, the tenth contract in the physical AI lineage)\index{Trajectory Plan!contract record}\index{Cyber-physical contract!trajectory planning}, immutable and handed over at every replanning cycle, makes that decision possible. The trajectory record is not merely a data serialization schema or ROS message definition; it is a formal **Cyber-Physical Contract** binding the high-level planner to explicit, auditable physical assumptions.

In the book's contract custody chain, the Trajectory Plan consumes two upstream contracts: the **Scene Memory State** (`SceneMemoryState`, Contract 8 from @sec-memory), from which it ingests the 3D Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF), voxel occupancy epochs, and raycasted free-space clearances; and the **Intent Specification** (`IntentSpecification`, Contract 9 from @sec-intent), from which it ingests the grounded semantic goal set, task tolerance bounds, effort ceilings, and parent intent lease digest. In return, the Trajectory Plan synthesizes a time-indexed, kinodynamically validated motion proposal that downstream @sec-enforcement ingests to evaluate Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) and emit per-tick **Admitted Commands** (`AdmittedCommand`, Contract 11).

If the physical plant violates declared bounds—such as payload mass, contact impedance, surface friction, or ODD geometry—the contract is breached, and TRACK authority is revoked immediately by the safety MCU. None of its nominal setpoints is admitted unless the record's matched stop suffix is resident and feasible from every state reachable before $t_{\text{commit}}$. It answers to the intent lease of @sec-intent-lease, whose digest it carries as its parent, and every setpoint it proposes pursues the lease's target without exceeding its effort ceilings. The record stores the motion as setpoint arrays or spline coefficients, together with the sample cadence (on this machine a `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_period_str` period $\Delta t_{\text{step}}$, a `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.f_step_str` setpoint stream), the nominal end $t_{\mathrm{plan\_exp}}$ (`{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp_str` for one chunk), and SI units. With the frame and evidence time of @sec-planning-handoff, the units, and the cadence in the handoff, the joint controller interpolates setpoints and evaluates derivatives without frame mismatches or reliance on ambient system clocks.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Trajectory feasibility proposals are separately checked against conditional control barrier functions in @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission.
:::

Physical feasibility depends on the scene and load used to validate the plan. The immutable sidecar therefore identifies obstacle-map epochs, payload and friction assumptions, limits, validator version, measured margin, and the source observation, and a digest in the fixed header binds it to the setpoints. The validator proves the stop feasible only under these assumptions, and they may claim no more than evaluation sampled, so the payload and friction the sidecar declares must lie inside the target Operational Design Domain (ODD) of @sec-evaluation-logs. The permission path revokes TRACK when live state leaves them, since a recorded margin holds only for the scene it was computed against. Solver seed and model hash belong in the audit sidecar for reproducibility where the toolchain supports it, not in the servo's per-tick path.

On this machine the chunk policy's output supplies only the nominal part of each trajectory record. Planning adds the seam state, the four deadlines, and the matched stop suffix, so the permission path admits one stream of records. The fixed header groups each record's fields by purpose. Lineage fields give a sequence number, the evidence time $t_0$, and the digest of the parent intent lease. Timing fields give the four deadlines of @sec-planning-handoff, and the record's tracking authority ends at the earliest of its commitment deadline, the lapse of the chunk lease (@sec-nervous-cadences) `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` after the last admitted chunk, the parent intent's expiry, and target-evidence expiry. Seam fields give the frame, each joint's entry state $(q,\dot q,\ddot q)$, and the stop-suffix coefficients. Content fields give the payload kind and size and one digest over the setpoint payload and the sidecar. A variable-length setpoint payload and immutable provenance/assumption sidecar are outside the fixed header, and the MCU verifies their digest before the admission check of @sec-planning-behavior-seam. The payload digest binds content, and the parent digest binds lineage. The record carries no keyed tag, because the permission path admits a proposal by its content rather than its origin (@sec-nervous-cadences).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Byte layout:** The trajectory record's field offsets and sizes are given in @sec-appendix-systems-wire-trajectory.
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-record-trace
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FILLED TRAJECTORY RECORD FOR THE REACH TOWARD THE MUG
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-trajectory-contract (filled record paragraph).
# │
# │ Goal:    Gather the worked record's field values from the cells that own
# │          them and add the one sidecar value no earlier cell holds.
# │ Show:    3 kg payload bound; 16 x 20 ms = 320 ms nominal end.
# │ How:     RM arm payload capacity; the other fields read
# │          PlanningLeaseRule, PlanningArmTimeline, and PlanningC2Stop.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import kilogram
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_mass

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlanningRecordTrace:
    """Sidecar payload bound for the worked trajectory record."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    m_payload = RM.arm.payload_capacity  # category: datasheet; arm payload capacity, registry

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_nominal = (PlanningArmTimeline.n_horizon * PlanningArmTimeline.t_period).to(PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp.units)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(m_payload.to(kilogram).magnitude - 3.0) < 1e-9, "arm payload capacity changed")
    check(t_nominal == PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp, "nominal end disagrees with horizon x period")
    check(PlanningLeaseRule.lease_total <= PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear, "lease-path stop no longer inside the clearance")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    m_payload_str = fmt_mass(m_payload, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
```

Filled in for one reach toward the mug, the record is the timeline of @fig-11-seam-timeline-fallback with its fields named. Its parent is the mug's intent lease, bound by digest; its frame is the machine's base frame, and every time field is in the MCU monotonic clock. Measured from $t_{\mathrm{start}}$, the timing fields hold the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str` commitment, the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp_str` nominal end that `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.n_horizon_str` setpoints at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_period_str` give, and the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_end_str` stop end; the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_blend_str` blend deadline is the schedule's target, not a field. The seam fields hold a `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_arm_stop_str` $C^2$ suffix that peaks at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_arm_peak_str` and brings the arm to rest from its `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_arm_str` TCP limit in `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_stop_dist_str`. While the record is in force, the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` chunk lease bounds its tracking, a lapse leads to the state-matched fallback along a path that uses `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_total_str` of the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear_str` clearance, and commitment caps that lease at `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_max_str`. The sidecar declares a payload of at most `{python} PlanningRecordTrace.m_payload_str`, free space until the grasp, and a scene inside the target ODD. Each field is one the permission path checks at admission or monitors on every tick, without asking the planner what it meant.

In the worked case the deadlines satisfy $t_{\mathrm{start}}\le t_{\mathrm{commit}}<t_{\mathrm{plan\_exp}}<t_{\mathrm{stop\_end}}$. The MCU applies these deadlines under the TRACK and STOP rules of @sec-planning-handoff, and a header timestamp cannot make a mismatched suffix safe. A log records evidence, request, validation, admission, activation, transfer, and stop-completion times in a common converted domain so actual response delay can be measured.

Every record in the runtime chain, from the observation contract through the belief record and the intent lease to the trajectory record itself, now names what it rests on and when it expires. The trajectory record proves only what the planner could foresee, a stop feasible from the states reachable before commitment under the scene and load in its sidecar. Several of the fallacies that follow mistake that bounded proof for a broader one.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-planning-fallacies-pitfalls}

A trajectory remains feasible only while its physical assumptions hold at chunk boundaries and during fallback. Admission and execution checks must address those transitions as well as the nominal path.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Static admission checks protect a machine against obstacle displacements during active execution.*

**Static geometry is an admission precondition, not an execution certificate; dynamic reality always requires runtime monitoring.** The arm begins an admitted reach toward the mug with the conveyor guard clear of its swept volume. During execution, a coworker slides a tote into the tool's path. The admission check was correct for the earlier geometry but no longer supports continued motion. Execution monitoring\index{Execution monitoring!collision detection} must detect the changed clearance and begin deceleration while sufficient stopping room remains. The design must bound how quickly workspace changes become visible via sensor bus latency\index{Network!bus latency} and reserve the stopping margin needed to respond before the updated geometry becomes impossible to avoid.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Couple static pre-execution spatial screening with a real-time swept-volume collision monitor running on the safety MCU. If an unmodeled obstacle breaches the reserved spatial margin $\epsilon_{\text{pos}}$, immediately abort nominal tracking and initiate the validated state-matched fallback.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Checking each action chunk alone without examining the motion the chunks compose.*

**Individual chunk feasibility does not imply composed trajectory stability; high-frequency reversals destroy transmissions.** The arm receives successive chunks that each reverse a joint's direction. Each chunk passes its own acceleration and jerk checks, yet the sequence produces oscillatory motion that can excite the drivetrain's resonant frequencies\index{Drivetrain!resonant frequency} through gearbox compliance\index{Gearbox!compliance}. Admission must compare derivatives across each seam and retain enough recent motion history to detect recurring reversals that would drive Joule heating ($I^2R$)\index{Motor!Joule heating} in the stator. The motor and transmission execute the composed trajectory, and treating chunks as independent requests hides behavior that appears only when the requests are joined.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Enforce multi-chunk frequency and reversal monitoring across the execution window. Reject or low-pass filter proposed chunk sequences whose direction-reversal cadence approaches the drivetrain's torsional antiresonance or thermal $I^2R$ accumulation threshold.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Delaying fallback transition past the hard stopping horizon in the hope that delayed compute finishes.*

**An overdue compute cycle never justifies extending a physical commitment deadline. Hope is not a deceleration profile.** With the lease run to its `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_max_str` ceiling, the worked arm's record ends its nominal setpoints at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp_str` and carries a `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_str` matched stop suffix that must finish by `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_end_str`, so the MCU must commit to fallback\index{Fallback trajectory!commitment point} at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str` unless it has admitted a valid replacement. At that point the application processor reports inference nearly complete, but it has not delivered an executable plan. Waiting spends the runway reserved for deceleration. The MCU must follow the matched stop suffix at the commitment point. Progress reports cannot extend a mechanical stopping budget; only a newly validated trajectory can justify continued execution.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Bind the commitment deadline $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$ strictly to the MCU monotonic hardware timer. When the timer expires without an admitted successor in the staging buffer, execute the pre-latched $C^2$ stopping suffix immediately, ignoring host progress updates.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Relying solely on feedforward dynamic models when physical contact or payload mass can change abruptly.*

**Feedforward model inversion without closed-loop disturbance bounds turns payload loss into explosive runaway.** The arm lifts an item near its `{python} PlanningRecordTrace.m_payload_str` payload bound using feedforward torque\index{Feedforward control!torque demand} computed for the loaded arm. The item slips from the gripper, but the drives keep applying the same lifting torque to the now unloaded arm, so it accelerates upward. The admitted trajectory has not changed; the dynamics that made its commands appropriate have. Feedback monitoring\index{Feedback control!error monitoring} must detect the resulting tracking error and constrain the commands within the available margin before a mechanical limit strike or thermal derating\index{Motor!thermal derating}. A feedforward model improves nominal tracking, but it cannot replace runtime checks for abrupt changes in payload or contact.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Implement real-time torque and tracking error monitoring ($\|\mathbf{x}_{\text{actual}} - \mathbf{x}_{\text{ref}}\| \le \epsilon_{\text{track}}$) at the 1 kHz servo layer. If sudden payload detachment or contact mismatch causes acceleration to spike, clamp motor currents and transition to compliance or emergency stop.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *A trajectory can omit an achievable terminal stopping suffix if replacement plans are expected to arrive in time.*

**A trajectory without a pre-latched stopping continuation is an unhedged bet on infinite compute availability.** At its `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_drive_str` drive limit, the mobile manipulator's base needs a $C^2$ suffix of $T=1.5v_c/a_{\text{brake}}$, `{python} PlanningC2Stop.c2_drive_time_str` at the credible `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_brake_str`, to stop without exceeding that deceleration.\index{Trajectory!braking time} A proposed suffix sized by the constant-deceleration time $v_c/a_{\text{brake}}$ is a third shorter, so its profile peaks at $1.5a_{\text{brake}}$, past what the loaded rack tolerates. Expecting the next plan to arrive does not make this fallback executable. The admission gate must check $T_{\mathrm{stop}} \ge 1.5\,v_c/a_{\text{brake}}$ for the $C^2$ profile it latches and reject a record that fails. Every accepted trajectory needs a physically achievable termination path\index{Fallback trajectory!achievability} for the case in which no replacement becomes available.

**Architect's countermeasure**: Require every candidate trajectory record to include complete, closed-form $C^2$ stopping polynomial coefficients satisfying $T_{\mathrm{stop}} \ge 1.5 v_c / a_{\text{brake}}$ within available clearance. Reject any record at the admission gate that lacks this independently executable return ticket.

:::

## Summary {#sec-planning-summary}

A trajectory is a timed proposal, and what shapes it is the case in which the next one is late. An inference-latency quantile is a scheduling risk target, not a safety certificate. It sets how often the machine should expect a late replacement, and the resident stop is what the machine does when one comes due. Two clocks bound the horizon from opposite sides. The compute tail pushes the commitment point later, while target evidence expires on its own schedule; on the conveyor, even a tracked observation of the mug expires before the worked `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str` commitment (@sec-intent-goals-expire), so tracking that long needs fresh evidence rather than a later timestamp.

Commitment is where these results meet. A replacement must pass full admission before $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$, not merely before the last nominal setpoint. On this machine the shared `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` lease ends a stall long before then and sends the arm to its state-matched fallback with `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_margin_str` of clearance left; commitment caps that lease at `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_max_str`, and a record that reaches commitment without a successor plays the $C^2$ suffix the MCU latched before motion began. The worked arm's `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_cruise_str` of cruise and `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_stop_dist_str` suffix leave `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` of geometric margin before uncertainty and unreserved delay. On the mobile manipulator's base, the suffix the tote rack tolerates raises the stopping budget at the drive limit to `{python} PlanningC2Stop.total_new_str`, past the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Timed motion and independent stopping"}
* **A latency quantile is a risk target**: The design-tail replacement target allocates the risk of a late plan and never certifies arrival, so every admitted trajectory carries a resident stop for the miss.
* **Commit before the runway is spent**: Admission closes at $t_{\mathrm{commit}}$, the deadline chosen so the matched stop still fits, and commitment caps the chunk lease that ends a stall first. On the arm, a lease run `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_wait_str` past commitment breaches the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_arm_clear_str` clearance by `{python} PlanningC2Stop.late_breach_arm_str`.
* **Evidence age and the compute tail pull apart**: A long tail pushes commitment later while target evidence expires on its own clock. Tracking past the evidence horizon needs a fresh observation, never a stretched timestamp.
* **A gentle stop is a longer stop**: A $C^2$ stop at the same peak deceleration travels half again the constant-deceleration distance, and on the mobile manipulator adding that term carries the budget past the rack-end clear distance at the drive limit.
* **The stage that first sees a failure owns it**: An invalid chunk, an infeasible seam, and a changed world first become visible at admission, at the seam, and during motion, so each stage holds its own signal and its own time budget for rejecting the plan.
* **Continuity is not feasibility**: A $C^2$ seam removes reference jumps, but the bridge's interior jerk, torque, resonance, and clearance must still be checked against the actual drive.
* **The planner proposes, the MCU admits**: The trajectory record binds setpoints, deadlines, and stop coefficients under its parent lease's digest, so the permission path judges the proposal by its content and holds a stop no host failure can erase.
:::

Trajectory generation represents the critical bridge where temporal predictions meet continuous mechanical dynamics. In classical motion planning, paths are solved over static geometric maps with the assumption that computation is an offline prerequisite. In Physical AI, high-capacity neural policies continuously generate receding-horizon action chunks while the machine hurtles through space with nonzero momentum. Time does not pause for optimization. Systems engineering resolves this fundamental tension by structuring planning as an unhedged contract: every admitted trajectory chunk must carry its own return ticket—a certified, dynamically feasible $C^2$ stopping suffix pre-latched in real-time memory. By binding motion proposals to rigorous commitment deadlines, the architecture guarantees that a computational stall or late replacement plan never converts into blind physical collision. With planned trajectories verified against kinematic limits and stopping clearance, the execution pipeline descends to the final real-time arbiter: the kilohertz enforcement loop.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From admitted plans to per-tick permission"}
This chapter admits whole proposals. The MCU checks a complete trajectory and its matched stop before commitment and latches the stop in protected memory. Admission judges the plan against the state the machine was in when the plan arrived, yet while the plan runs the plant can lag its reference, an obstacle can appear, and an actuator can saturate. @Sec-enforcement checks each tick against live state, insets the stopping distance by the tracking error the controller can bound, and owns the fallback ladder whose stop rung plays this chapter's resident stop. That inset is the last term of the machine's stopping budget, and adding it sets the speed at which the mobile manipulator may run the aisle.
:::
